demographics.trauma_type: Accidentally caused serious injury to another

Triggers.value: Physical pain in a part of the body

Threat.value: I am unable to relax even when I know I am in a safe place
I feel threatened by strangers approaching me even in ordinary situations
I watch other people closely for signs that they might harm me

Memory.value: When memories come to mind of what happened, I feel my body is in the same position as when the frightening event occurred.
When I remember the event I feel intense rage
When I remember the event I feel overwhelming grief

Negative Appraisals.value: There is something about me that made the event happen
I am no longer capable of doing the things that defined me

vignette: Marcus, a 54-year-old forester from Oregon, had always found solace in the tranquility of the forest. His days were filled with the sounds of rustling leaves and the smell of damp earth, but all of that changed one fateful day when a tragic accident occurred while he was working. During a routine task of clearing fallen branches, he accidentally caused a severe injury to a fellow worker, a close friend who had been helping him. Marcus vividly recalled the moment everything changed: the crack of the branch breaking, the agonizing cry of his friend, and the chaos that followed. Since that day, he had been haunted by memories that often flared up unexpectedly. Simple triggers, like the sound of cracking wood or the sight of someone in distress, would send Marcus's heart racing and his body tensing, as if reliving the trauma. Each time he encountered these reminders, he felt an overwhelming sense of threat. The jolt of anxiety that accompanied these triggers made him feel as though danger was imminent, reinforcing his belief that he could never truly be safe again. The sound of cracking wood or the sight of someone in distress would send his mind racing, amplifying the perception that danger was imminent, making it impossible for him to feel secure in his surroundings. These triggers not only heightened his anxiety but also led him to internalize negative appraisals of himself, convincing him that he was incapable of managing his surroundings and that safety was forever out of reach. The sound of cracking wood or the sight of someone in distress would drag him back to the moment of the accident, flooding his mind with memories of chaos and pain, making him feel as if he were reliving the trauma all over again. Each time those memories surged, they felt more vivid and real, further amplifying his sense of threat, as if he were still trapped in that moment of chaos. This relentless cycle of triggers and memories only served to heighten his sense of threat, as the past felt ever-present, and the danger of it all loomed larger with each reminder. These cues led to a feeling of danger that felt as real as the original event, making him hyper-aware of his surroundings and amplifying his anxiety. Strangers approaching him while he worked in the forest made him jumpy; he felt as though they might be hostile, even when they were simply passing by. The everyday world became a source of anxiety, leaving him unable to relax, even in the safety of his own home. These triggers were not just fleeting moments; they had become a pervasive part of Marcus's life. He found himself avoiding social gatherings and steering clear of crowded places, certain that he would feel suffocated by the memories of his friend's injury. He would often replay the scene in his mind, feeling as though he were back in that moment, his body mimicking the physical position he had held when the accident occurred. The vividness of these memories would often be triggered by the simplest of cues, like the sound of cracking wood or someone in distress, dragging him back into the chaos and pain of that day. In those moments, the memories would flood his mind, each scene sparking a cascade of negative thoughts about his worthiness and ability to cope, deepening his feelings of inadequacy. Each cue pulled him deeper into the past, as the familiar sounds and sights would ignite the memories of that horrific day, making the trauma feel as fresh as when it first occurred. With every recollection, the nagging thought would surface - that he was fundamentally flawed and responsible for the pain, reinforcing his negative self-appraisal. Every time a memory bubbled up, it would remind him of his perceived failures, leading him to believe even more strongly that he was not the dependable person he once was, deepening his feelings of inadequacy. With each intrusive thought, Marcus was reminded of his perceived failures, leading him to believe that he could never be safe again, further entrenching the negative self-beliefs that haunted him. The reminders of his friend's injury would often surface alongside those negative thoughts, convincing him that he was fundamentally flawed and incapable of handling responsibilities, reinforcing his sense of inadequacy. Each memory was a reminder of his perceived failure, igniting intense feelings of rage at himself for allowing it to happen. These memories solidified his negative self-beliefs, leading him to think that he would never be able to regain his previous competence or safety in his work. Each recollection reinforced the belief that he was at fault, leading him to conclude that he was no longer capable of performing his job safely or effectively. Every time those memories resurfaced, they would echo in his mind, amplifying the belief that he had let everyone down, intensifying the negative self-appraisal that he was not the dependable person he once was. The memories surfaced not just as echoes of the past, but as affirmations of his worst fears, convincing him that he was fundamentally flawed and incapable of handling the responsibilities he once embraced. This cycle of remembering and self-blame deepened his conviction that he could never regain his previous competence, making him feel trapped in a life devoid of safety and self-worth. The anger often morphed into deep, overwhelming grief, leaving him drained and hollow. These feelings were compounded by a relentless inner voice that told him he was at fault, that there was something intrinsically wrong with him, something that made the accident inevitable. He believed he could no longer rely on himself; the man who had once confidently navigated the forest now felt lost, a shadow of his former self. As Marcus's memories resurfaced, they not only triggered emotional turmoil but also deepened his negative self-appraisals. Each recollection reinforced his belief that he was no longer capable of performing his job safely or effectively. He had once taken pride in his work, but now he felt like a danger not just to himself but to others as well. The weight of these thoughts made it difficult for him to engage in even the most mundane tasks, perpetuating a cycle of avoidance and despair. He would sit at home, ruminating over the past, while his wife, Claire, tried to reach out to him. The distance between them grew as he withdrew from conversations, fearing that discussing the accident might lead to more painful memories. It was a cruel irony, as he longed to be the man he once was, yet felt shackled by the very events that had defined his recent existence. Caught in this cycle of triggers and memories, the sense of threat only grew stronger. This sense of threat heightened his anxiety, as each encounter made him hyper-aware of the potential for danger, fueling his instinct to withdraw and avoid any interactions that might escalate. Even in familiar surroundings, he felt a hyper-awareness of his environment, watching others closely, anticipating harm where there was none. This constant vigilance was a direct response to the perceived threat, as he believed that danger lurked in every corner, solidifying the idea that he was forever on high alert, unable to relax. This persistent sense of threat only served to reinforce the negative beliefs he held about himself, convincing him that he was not the kind of person who could ever feel safe again. In this heightened state of watchfulness, every unfamiliar sound or sight would pull him back into the trauma, as the adrenaline triggered memories of chaos and pain. This threat made every ordinary situation feel loaded with the possibility of disaster, turning even simple activities into breeding grounds for anxiety and intrusive memories of the accident. In moments of heightened anxiety, the memories would bubble to the surface, pulling him back into the chaos of that day, making it feel as though he was reliving the trauma over and over again. This constant state of vigilance only served to intensify his feelings of inadequacy, as he grappled with the fear that he could not protect himself or anyone else. The persistent sense of danger confirmed the thought he worked hardest to resist - that this was simply who he was now, someone incapable of feeling safe. Each time he felt that threat, it reinforced the notion that he was living in a new reality, one where the past had irrevocably altered him, fostering a deep sense of helplessness. This constant vigilance led him to believe that he was a burden to those around him, reinforcing the notion that he could never be the dependable person he once was. Each encounter felt like an echo of the accident, and the physical manifestations of his pain-tightness in his chest, a knot in his stomach-reminded him that the emotional scars were as real as the physical ones he had witnessed that day. Walking through the forest, he would often be reminded of that day, as if his body instinctively recalled the trauma, prompting him to avoid any situation that could lead to a similar experience. The constant threat he felt made even the simplest activities feel charged with potential danger, turning his everyday environment into a minefield of triggers that could pull him back into the trauma. The persistent fear that accompanied these memories left him feeling trapped; he avoided the forest and any reminders of the accident, convinced that he could never escape the grip of his trauma. The echoes of that memory created an ever-present sense of threat in the forest, turning it from a place of solace into a landscape fraught with the potential for danger. The forest, once a place of peace, now felt fraught with triggers, as the familiar sounds and sights evoked a sense of impending danger that made it impossible for him to relax. Each time he encountered these reminders, they brought with them an overwhelming sense of threat, making him feel as though danger was imminent and that he was once again trapped in a moment of chaos. Finally, after months of suffering in silence, Marcus sought help. He was overwhelmed by the sense that if he didn't address the threat that shadowed him daily, he would remain forever stuck in a cycle of fear and regret. He sat in the therapist's office, feeling a mixture of hope and dread. He was terrified of confronting the pain but equally terrified of remaining trapped in a life defined by his trauma. What he hoped for most was a way to reclaim his sense of self and to learn how to navigate the world without the shadow of fear looming over him. As he began to articulate his struggles, he realized he was not alone; acknowledging the weight of his experience was the first step toward healing.

vignette_attempts.feedback:
REQUIRED EDGES MISSING:
- Triggers → Threat: The vignette does not explain how triggers lead to a sense of threat.
  e.g. "The cues led to a feeling of danger that felt as real as the original event."
  e.g. "A knock at the door after dark sent her heart into her throat — her body read it as an emergency, even when her mind knew better."
  e.g. "Sitting in the waiting room, she noticed a man watching her from across the room and felt the same cold certainty: something terrible was about to happen."
- Triggers → Memory: The vignette does not explain how triggers lead to memory.
  e.g. "The smell of his cologne in the lift sent the whole night flooding back before she had even reached her floor."
  e.g. "Hearing that song on the radio dragged her straight back into the room where it happened, as if no time had passed at all."
  e.g. "Walking past the bus stop where it occurred, she was no longer on the street — she was back there, every detail sharp and close."
- Triggers → Negative Appraisals: The vignette does not explain how triggers lead to negative appraisals.
  e.g. "Every time she walked through that car park, the thought arrived with her: this is what your life is now — flinching at nothing."
  e.g. "Seeing a man in the same jacket made her think, with quiet certainty, that she would never stop being afraid."
  e.g. "The sound of raised voices next door told her, with a logic she couldn't argue with, that nowhere was ever really safe."
- Memory → Negative Appraisals: The vignette does not explain how memory leads to negative appraisals.
  e.g. "After the image broke through again, she caught herself thinking: if this keeps happening, there must be something deeply wrong with me."
  e.g. "The memory surfaced in the middle of a meeting and she spent the rest of the day convinced that everyone around her could see how broken she was."
  e.g. "Each time the flashback came, the thought that followed it was always the same — that she had let this happen, and that it said something permanent about who she was."
- Threat → Memory: The vignette does not explain how threat leads to memory.
  e.g. "Walking home on high alert, she passed a doorway and the memory was simply there — pulled out of her by the adrenaline, fully formed."
  e.g. "The persistent sense of danger kept her close to the event in her mind, as if she needed to keep reviewing it to stay one step ahead of whatever came next."
  e.g. "On nights when the threat felt highest, the memory was hardest to keep at bay — it would surface in the dark, vivid and unwelcome."
- Threat → Negative Appraisals: The vignette does not explain how threat leads to negative appraisals.
  e.g. "The constant sense of danger was the most convincing proof she had that her life had changed beyond repair."
  e.g. "Feeling this afraid all the time, she had eventually come to accept the conclusion her body kept offering: that she was not the kind of person who got to feel safe."
  e.g. "The threat that shadowed her days quietly confirmed the thought she worked hardest to resist — that this was simply who she was now."
- Threat → Triggers: The vignette does not explain how threat leads to triggers.
  e.g. "Already running on threat, she found that almost anything could tip into a warning — a van parked at an odd angle, a light left on that shouldn't have been."
  e.g. "The background hum of danger she carried everywhere made ordinary cues feel like messages — each one confirming what her body already believed."
  e.g. "Living at that pitch of alertness, she found the world had become dense with reminders she couldn't stop reading."

vignette_attempts.vignette: Marcus, a 54-year-old forester from Oregon, had always found solace in the tranquility of the forest. His days were filled with the sounds of rustling leaves and the smell of damp earth, but all of that changed one fateful day when a tragic accident occurred while he was working. During a routine task of clearing fallen branches, he accidentally caused a severe injury to a fellow worker, a close friend who had been helping him. Marcus vividly recalled the moment everything changed: the crack of the branch breaking, the agonizing cry of his friend, and the chaos that followed. Since that day, he had been haunted by memories that often flared up unexpectedly. Simple triggers, like the sound of cracking wood or the sight of someone in distress, would send Marcus's heart racing and his body tensing, as if reliving the trauma. Each time he encountered these reminders, he felt an overwhelming sense of threat. The sound of cracking wood or the sight of someone in distress would send his mind racing, amplifying the perception that danger was imminent, making it impossible for him to feel secure in his surroundings. The sound of cracking wood or the sight of someone in distress would drag him back to the moment of the accident, flooding his mind with memories of chaos and pain, making him feel as if he were reliving the trauma all over again. This relentless cycle of triggers and memories only served to heighten his sense of threat, as the past felt ever-present, and the danger of it all loomed larger with each reminder. These cues led to a feeling of danger that felt as real as the original event, making him hyper-aware of his surroundings and amplifying his anxiety. Strangers approaching him while he worked in the forest made him jumpy; he felt as though they might be hostile, even when they were simply passing by. The everyday world became a source of anxiety, leaving him unable to relax, even in the safety of his own home. These triggers were not just fleeting moments; they had become a pervasive part of Marcus's life. He found himself avoiding social gatherings and steering clear of crowded places, certain that he would feel suffocated by the memories of his friend’s injury. He would often replay the scene in his mind, feeling as though he were back in that moment, his body mimicking the physical position he had held when the accident occurred. The vividness of these memories would often be triggered by the simplest of cues, like the sound of cracking wood or someone in distress, dragging him back into the chaos and pain of that day. Each cue pulled him deeper into the past, as the familiar sounds and sights would ignite the memories of that horrific day, making the trauma feel as fresh as when it first occurred. With each intrusive thought, Marcus was reminded of his perceived failures, leading him to believe that he could never be safe again, further entrenching the negative self-beliefs that haunted him. The reminders of his friend's injury would often surface alongside those negative thoughts, convincing him that he was fundamentally flawed and incapable of handling responsibilities, reinforcing his sense of inadequacy. Each memory was a reminder of his perceived failure, igniting intense feelings of rage at himself for allowing it to happen. Each recollection reinforced the belief that he was at fault, leading him to conclude that he was no longer capable of performing his job safely or effectively. Every time those memories resurfaced, they would echo in his mind, amplifying the belief that he had let everyone down, intensifying the negative self-appraisal that he was not the dependable person he once was. The memories surfaced not just as echoes of the past, but as affirmations of his worst fears, convincing him that he was fundamentally flawed and incapable of handling the responsibilities he once embraced. This cycle of remembering and self-blame deepened his conviction that he could never regain his previous competence, making him feel trapped in a life devoid of safety and self-worth. The anger often morphed into deep, overwhelming grief, leaving him drained and hollow. These feelings were compounded by a relentless inner voice that told him he was at fault, that there was something intrinsically wrong with him, something that made the accident inevitable. He believed he could no longer rely on himself; the man who had once confidently navigated the forest now felt lost, a shadow of his former self. As Marcus's memories resurfaced, they not only triggered emotional turmoil but also deepened his negative self-appraisals. Each recollection reinforced his belief that he was no longer capable of performing his job safely or effectively. He had once taken pride in his work, but now he felt like a danger not just to himself but to others as well. The weight of these thoughts made it difficult for him to engage in even the most mundane tasks, perpetuating a cycle of avoidance and despair. He would sit at home, ruminating over the past, while his wife, Claire, tried to reach out to him. The distance between them grew as he withdrew from conversations, fearing that discussing the accident might lead to more painful memories. It was a cruel irony, as he longed to be the man he once was, yet felt shackled by the very events that had defined his recent existence. Caught in this cycle of triggers and memories, the sense of threat only grew stronger. This sense of threat heightened his anxiety, as each encounter made him hyper-aware of the potential for danger, fueling his instinct to withdraw and avoid any interactions that might escalate. Even in familiar surroundings, he felt a hyper-awareness of his environment, watching others closely, anticipating harm where there was none. This constant vigilance was a direct response to the perceived threat, as he believed that danger lurked in every corner, solidifying the idea that he was forever on high alert, unable to relax. This threat made every ordinary situation feel loaded with the possibility of disaster, turning even simple activities into breeding grounds for anxiety and intrusive memories of the accident. In moments of heightened anxiety, the memories would bubble to the surface, pulling him back into the chaos of that day, making it feel as though he was reliving the trauma over and over again. This constant state of vigilance only served to intensify his feelings of inadequacy, as he grappled with the fear that he could not protect himself or anyone else. The persistent sense of danger confirmed the thought he worked hardest to resist — that this was simply who he was now, someone incapable of feeling safe. Each time he felt that threat, it reinforced the notion that he was living in a new reality, one where the past had irrevocably altered him, fostering a deep sense of helplessness. This constant vigilance led him to believe that he was a burden to those around him, reinforcing the notion that he could never be the dependable person he once was. Each encounter felt like an echo of the accident, and the physical manifestations of his pain—tightness in his chest, a knot in his stomach—reminded him that the emotional scars were as real as the physical ones he had witnessed that day. Walking through the forest, he would often be reminded of that day, as if his body instinctively recalled the trauma, prompting him to avoid any situation that could lead to a similar experience. The echoes of that memory created an ever-present sense of threat in the forest, turning it from a place of solace into a landscape fraught with the potential for danger. The forest, once a place of peace, now felt fraught with triggers, as the familiar sounds and sights evoked a sense of impending danger that made it impossible for him to relax. Finally, after months of suffering in silence, Marcus sought help. He sat in the therapist's office, feeling a mixture of hope and dread. He was terrified of confronting the pain but equally terrified of remaining trapped in a life defined by his trauma. What he hoped for most was a way to reclaim his sense of self and to learn how to navigate the world without the shadow of fear looming over him. As he began to articulate his struggles, he realized he was not alone; acknowledging the weight of his experience was the first step toward healing.
